interest: For historians of diplomacy, sports, and U.S.-East Asian relations, this file offers a fascinating window into early grassroots 'sports diplomacy' during a period of escalating geopolitical friction between the United States and Japan. It reveals how private promoters sought to leverage shared athletic culture—specifically the enormous popularity of baseball—to ease bilateral tensions and foster international goodwill, anticipating later public diplomacy initiatives. Additionally, the internal memoranda provide valuable insight into the institutional mindset of the State Department, illustrating how diplomats like Stanley K. Hornbeck and Ransford S. Miller carefully navigated the boundary between encouraging cultural exchange and upholding strict institutional prohibitions against endorsing private commercial enterprises.
overview: This file (State Department decimal 894.40634, File 919) covers the years 1930 to 1936 and consists of correspondence, memoranda, telegrams, and cross-reference sheets centered on proposals by United Press journalist Henry F. Misselwitz to establish professional baseball in Japan and inaugurate an annual international World Series between American and Japanese champions. Spanning both the Hoover and Roosevelt administrations, the records document Misselwitz’s repeated lobbying of Secretaries of State Henry L. Stimson and Cordell Hull, as well as White House Assistant Secretary Stephen T. Early and Far Eastern Affairs officials, seeking official or informal endorsements to bolster his sporting enterprise and promote Japanese-American goodwill. In response, State Department officials consistently maintained a strict policy against lending the prestige of the U.S. government or its officials' names to private commercial ventures, while expressing informal sympathy for athletic exchange, alongside brief cross-references noting amateur exchanges such as the Harvard University baseball team tours in Japan.
